video_title: Why AI Is Reinventing How Businesses Buy Everything
gist: a16z partner Sema Amble and LEO CEO Vlad Kyle argue AI-native startups beat incumbents-plus-models by owning end-to-end, judgment-heavy work that lives outside systems of record, using enterprise procurement as the case: multi-agent systems autonomously negotiate tail spend under ~$50k, handle exceptions (80% of the job), and augment 3-month direct-procurement negotiations. Key claims: DIY builds stall at 70-80% accuracy, pricing judgment needs proprietary outcome-trained models, and 1% procurement savings equals ~10% more revenue.

insights.claim: AI-native startups beat incumbent software vendors that bolt models onto their system of record because incumbents stay confined to that single record and do not complete the end-to-end job, which spans billing, chat history, contracts and other systems.
insights.speaker: Sema Amble (a16z partner)
insights.so_what: Back startups that own full workflows across systems; discount 'incumbent + LLM' threat for cross-system work.
insights.quote: the legacy incumbent is limited to their system of record and that record that they have and they're not completing the endto-end job

insights.claim: The classic startup-vs-incumbent 'distribution vs innovation' fight now has a third element: incumbents layering frontier models on top (e.g. a Claude-plus-Salesforce combination), making them a much more formidable competitor.
insights.speaker: Sema Amble (a16z partner)
insights.so_what: Raises the bar for thin AI wrappers in categories where the incumbent owns data and seats.

insights.claim: A four-stage agent taxonomy distinguishes retrieval agents (fetch/synthesize data), process agents (execute rule-based steps with no judgment), policy agents (apply judgment where rules are ambiguous), and principal agents (weigh business trade-offs such as relationship value beyond policy).
insights.speaker: Sema Amble (a16z partner)
insights.so_what: Useful lens to grade how far up the judgment stack a vendor actually operates.

insights.claim: Most incumbents started, if at all, with retrieval-style 'slap on a chatbot' products and, despite marketing about process and policy agents, their launched workflow agents remain limited to retrieval and light process with no real judgment.
insights.speaker: Sema Amble (a16z partner)
insights.so_what: Incumbent AI marketing overstates capability; judgment-heavy agent markets remain open for startups.

insights.claim: Incumbents are structurally held back from judgment-level agents by internal incentive conflicts: a product that resolves work end to end cannibalizes workflow software sold to human agents, targets a different buyer, and pits separate VP-led orgs against each other in sales.
insights.speaker: Sema Amble (a16z partner)
insights.so_what: Innovator's-dilemma dynamics favor startups selling outcomes over seats.

insights.claim: Incumbents' distribution advantage is real: Salesforce's Agent Force was easy for customers to adopt because of existing trust and was offered at almost no extra cost.
insights.speaker: Sema Amble (a16z partner)
insights.so_what: Bundled/near-free incumbent agents compress pricing for retrieval-level point products.

insights.claim: Incumbents already hold customer trust but can destroy it by shipping immature agents too early, whereas startups must earn trust incrementally.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Asymmetric downside risk slows incumbent agent rollouts, widening the startup window.

insights.claim: Some incumbents are responding by partnering with OpenAI, Anthropic or other labs to supercharge their existing products with model capability.
insights.speaker: Sema Amble (a16z partner)
insights.so_what: Lab-incumbent partnerships are a key competitive variable for vertical AI startups.

themes.theme: Procurement work lives outside the ERP

insights.claim: Most procurement work happens outside the ERP or any system of record: a final '8K for aluminum' entry hides supplier pushback, weeks of cost-engineering spreadsheets and 3D modeling, dozens of stakeholder meetings and hundreds of emails.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: The data moat for procurement AI is unstructured context (email, Excel), not ERP records incumbents own.
insights.quote: most of the work um in procurement actually happens outside of this um ERP or any system of record

insights.claim: In large builds such as aircraft or data centers, a single part arriving two weeks late can cause hundreds of millions of dollars in damage, and such delay notices often sit unnoticed among ~500 emails in a procurement manager's inbox while the system of record only records a changed date.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Supply-chain exception detection on unstructured comms is a high-value, under-served AI use case.
insights.quote: if they missed this email hundreds of millions of damage done and this h like this happens regularly

insights.claim: Invoice-processing software as built today addresses 100% of the invoice software market but only about 20% of the actual job; ~80% of the problem is exception handling such as fraud and mismatches off the happy path.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Value in AP/procurement automation sits in exceptions; legacy happy-path tools are exposed.

insights.claim: Procurement is a cross-functional process involving legal (contract design), finance (payment/collection terms), cost engineering (cost structure) and procurement (commercials), with specialist staff who hold company- and industry-specific knowledge.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: End-to-end procurement agents expand TAM beyond the procurement department budget.

insights.claim: Direct procurement (parts that go into the product, e.g. airplanes, drones, robots) involves roughly 100 to 2,000 highly strategic suppliers, sometimes $1B of spend with one supplier, and negotiations lasting ~3 months, versus indirect procurement (MRO, factory build-out, laptops, marketing services) with tens of thousands of suppliers.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Different automation profiles: indirect is automation-led, direct is high-stakes expert augmentation.

insights.claim: In complex multi-million-dollar negotiations about 90% of the work is preparation, so agents act mainly back-of-house, though real-time assistance is emerging (e.g. flagging that a 10% oil index rise justifies only ~4% price increase when oil is 30% of the product).
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Preparation-heavy workflows are where agent labor substitution is largest.

insights.claim: Requesters outside procurement (e.g. a construction worker who opens a laptop every other week) cannot navigate SAP or ERP categories, GL accounts and framework contracts, so intake via photo, quote or spreadsheet upload is a key unlock.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Intake UX is a wedge; ERP complexity suppresses compliant spend capture.

themes.theme: LEO's multi-agent architecture and trust ramp

insights.claim: LEO runs a multi-agent system because a human-level procurement task involves about eight stakeholders, three departments and five software tools; a single agent could not negotiate without contract, news and other specialist agents sharing context in a specific order.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Signals architectural complexity as a barrier vs. single-agent incumbent add-ons.

insights.claim: For a standard part like a bolt, LEO can run fully autonomously end to end: intake, inventory check, cross-plant sourcing, supplier search, RFQ drafting and sending, parsing messy email/PDF/Excel replies, price benchmarking, choosing negotiation mode (human-in-loop, autonomous, or e-auction), order confirmation, shipment tracking and invoices.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Demonstrates full-cycle autonomy in indirect spend, implying labor-replacement pricing potential.

insights.claim: No enterprise starts with fully autonomous negotiation agents; LEO uses human-in-the-loop to learn each Fortune 10 customer's specific way of operating until trust scales to 10k, 20k, then 100k negotiations.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Human-in-the-loop is a data flywheel and trust ramp, key for enterprise agent adoption curves.
insights.quote: no company and no enterprise starts with fully autonomous negotiation agents from day one. No one does that.

insights.claim: Enterprises historically did not negotiate spend below about $50k due to lack of capacity, so autonomous negotiation agents capture previously unaddressed savings where the downside of a mediocre negotiation is near zero.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Tail-spend negotiation is a near-riskless, net-new savings pool and an easy ROI wedge.
insights.quote: you can just send um an enterprise an invoice for 40k they will probably not negotiate because they don't have the capacity to do so

insights.claim: LEO's product strategy is to stay slightly ahead of the capability curve: pitching the next generation of agents (retrieval three years ago, now long-running and fully autonomous agents) before the tech is fully ready, then shipping within weeks once demand is validated.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Speed of riding model capability gains is a key execution signal for vertical AI startups.

insights.claim: Supply risk can be managed probabilistically: with full context, an agent may choose a supplier 10x more expensive if it loses 1% of goods versus 20% for the cheaper one, and can incorporate external signals like news and Polymarket bets on disruptions.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Prediction-market and news data becoming inputs to enterprise supply decisions.

insights.claim: About 85% of LEO's staff are engineers, and forward-deployed engineers are measured on automating their own jobs to push customization toward self-service rather than becoming a consulting firm.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Indicates gross-margin discipline versus services-heavy AI deployments.
insights.quote: 85% of the people are um engineers

insights.claim: LEO treats foundation models from all providers as a commodity; a model plus a harness can reach 100% of some jobs, but tasks like should-cost modeling and price benchmarking plateau around 80% and require fine-tuning on proprietary data.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Moat shifts to proprietary pricing data and outcome-trained models, not model access.

insights.claim: Price benchmarking data is proprietary to enterprises and not publicly available, so general-purpose labs cannot train on it; LEO is exploring outcome-based models trained on text that output a price rather than a classic LLM.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Cross-enterprise pricing data could be a defensible network-effect asset.

insights.claim: Pricing judgment is tacit: two consulting quotes (e.g. BCG and McKinsey) for identical work can differ 10x, and an experienced procurement manager has a gut feeling about fair price that cannot be written down as rules, so harnesses fail and outcome-trained models are needed.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Tacit-knowledge tasks are where fine-tuned vertical models beat prompting general models.

insights.claim: Harvey and Decagon are cited as companies now fine-tuning models.
insights.speaker: Elena Burgerer (host)
insights.so_what: Fine-tuning is becoming standard among leading vertical AI apps.

insights.claim: LEO's first viral product (quote-to-SAP retrieval) took three to four engineers to build three years ago and is now an 8-hour take-home case study for job applicants, showing how cheap the basic build has become.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Retrieval-level features are commoditized; value must come from the last-mile accuracy.
insights.quote: this is nowadays a case study um if you if you're applying to work at LEO so we give this to people like to build this and they have like 8 hours to do so

insights.claim: In-house AI builds typically reach ~70-80% performance, but 70% accuracy does not mean 70% automation: humans must still check all outputs, so the work can increase; the last 20% (integrations, memory, workflows, vertical data) is ~80% of the effort.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Argues against 'enterprises will build it themselves' bear case for vertical AI.
insights.quote: 70% of performance or accuracy or however you measure it. It depends really on the task doesn't mean 70% um automation

insights.claim: A Fortune 500 company spent at least three to four months trying to build its own cash-collection AI and abandoned it due to poor-quality context and the burden of maintaining mappings across two ERPs plus a third from a pending acquisition.
insights.speaker: Sema Amble (a16z partner)
insights.so_what: Real-world evidence that DIY enterprise AI stalls, supporting vendor demand.

insights.claim: Broad adoption of base models and ChatGPT-style products is net positive for vertical AI vendors because it raises enterprise familiarity and trust in AI tools.
insights.speaker: Sema Amble (a16z partner)
insights.so_what: Lab consumer growth is a tailwind, not just a threat, to vertical apps.

insights.claim: Moats are hard to forecast early; the best early businesses focused on winning customer trust and expanding usage, and stickiness and network effects are downstream of customers becoming dependent on a product that does the work (e.g. a sales agent owning prep and outbound vs a CRM that logs deals).
insights.speaker: Sema Amble (a16z partner)
insights.so_what: Diligence should weight dependency/work-ownership over speculative moat narratives.
insights.quote: It's really really hard to forecast your moat going forward

insights.claim: AI enables per-customer customization without the old scaling penalty: forward-deployed work today is a learning loop that increasingly gets automated and exposed as customer-controlled settings, replacing Accenture-style SAP customization; incumbents struggle because implementation is an afterthought not feeding product.
insights.speaker: Sema Amble (a16z partner)
insights.so_what: Implementation services revenue pools (SIs) are at risk as deployment becomes software-driven.

themes.theme: Two-sided agents and procurement market size

insights.claim: Agents will exist on both buyer and supplier sides; contrary to the assumption that sales tech leads procurement, suppliers to Fortune 500 firms are not yet deploying work-automating agents.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Supplier-side agent adoption is an open greenfield.

insights.claim: Large industrial buyers (e.g. automotive OEMs) dictate tools, quality and RFQ response formats to suppliers, so a procurement platform can push suppliers onto its own agents and own both sides of the transaction.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Buyer-led network effects could turn a procurement SaaS into a two-sided marketplace.

insights.claim: Even if price negotiation is zero-sum, price is the outcome of ~5,000 other tasks where buyer and seller incentives align (speed, low friction, time to market), so one platform can serve both sides.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Supports cross-side platform plays; coordination value exceeds adversarial friction.
insights.quote: price is like the outcome of like 5,000 different like other task that happened and on those 5,000 other tasks they have the same incentive

insights.claim: Despite roughly 500 to 1,000 procurement tools, practitioners still work in email, Teams, Excel and PowerPoint with zero AI, because legacy tools only made processes more efficient without changing how people work; the last real revolution was ~20 years ago.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Fragmented, disliked legacy stack signals displacement opportunity in procurement software.

insights.claim: A 1% procurement savings is equivalent in P&L impact to roughly 10% more revenue, which underpins Vlad's view that procurement is a trillion-dollar business opportunity.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Clear ROI framing drives CFO-level buying and pricing power for procurement AI.
insights.quote: if you just manage to get like 1% savings it's like equals like 10% of sales

insights.claim: Categories that are boring, niche, highly emotional (users are frustrated) and have big P&L impact are attractive for AI startups because users are easy to amaze; procurement fits all three.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Screening heuristic for underserved enterprise AI verticals.

insights.claim: LEO's 'Bots and Buyers' procurement summit drew over 100 senior procurement leaders in New York on its third edition, with the next event in Munich expected at around 700 people.
insights.speaker: Vlad Kyle (LEO co-founder/CEO)
insights.so_what: Growing buyer engagement is a demand indicator for AI procurement.
